#2759. Panthers vs Broncos: Recap and reaction

The Carolina Panthers battled, but some bad penalties and bad luck resulted in a loss to the Denver Broncos, 26-20.

The Broncos got the ball first and immediately marched it down the field. They ran the kickoff out past the 40 then took two deep shots. Neither connected, but the second drew a rather ticky tack pass interference call. Jonah Coleman broke off a few nice runs to quickly put the Broncos in goal to go. The defense stepped up there. They stopped a first down run then got pressure on Bo Nix on second and third down to force incompletions and a fourth down field goal.

The Panthers offense did nothing outside of a first play completion to Mitchell Evans. The Broncos moved the ball quickly once again. A couple of chunk plays got them into Panthers territory. Lee Hunter had a couple of nice plays, but another pass interference extended the drive. A few plays later, Bo Nix hit Courtland Sutton on a quick slant for a touchdown.

The Panthers went three and out after a near miss to Tetairoa McMillan and a bad route by Darren Waller. After the punt, Marco Wilson got called for a taunting penalty for standing over Jaylen Waddle after an incomplete pass. The quarter ended after Bobby Brown led a group of Panthers in the backfield for a tackle for loss.

The defense got off the field on third and long to get the ball back. The offense finally moved into Denver territory with a completion to McMillan and a couple of good runs by Chuba Hubbard, the second of which drew a late hit at the end. The drive fell apart after that. Young was nearly picked by Riley Moss, then three players jumped early for a false start. They ultimately settled for a 43 yard field goal, which Ryan Fitzgerald pretty much shanked out to the right.

The Broncos moved the ball into Panthers territory, aided by a pass interference by Marco Wilson, his fourth penalty of the game. He was bailed out this time though. A couple plays later, Corey Thornton skied to undercut a receiver for an interception.

The momentum shifted a little bit from that point. Bryce Young picked up a 3rd and 15 with a deep comeback to McMillan. He found Darren Waller a few times over the middle to continue the march into Broncos territory. The offense was faced with a 4th and 1, and Chuba Hubbard broke free off the left side for a big game. A few plays later, Young found Tommy Tremble in the backfield corner of the end zone for a toe tapping touchdown.

Ryan Fitzgerald actually made the extra point this time, but he followed that by kicking the ensuing kickoff out of bounds. That gave the Broncos a short field to manage a quick two minute drill into field goal range to make it 13-7 heading into the half.

The Panthers got the ball first out of the half and carried their momentum from the end of the first half. Young found Waller out of the gate for a big gain. A nine yard run from Hubbard and a nine yard catch by Evans put the Panthers on the edge of the red zone. After a couple of ineffective plays, Young found Waller deep over the middle for a touchdown to put the Panthers up 14-13.

The defense kept the good vibes rolling. They stuffed a couple of early down runs to force the Broncos into an obvious passing situation. They got quick pressure, which forced Nix to step up into the waiting arms of Pat Jones.

Young continued to pick apart the Broncos defense with more help from Darren Waller. He also had a 15 yard scramble to help the drive along. The Panthers got inside the five. Young tried to find Tremble in the end zone, but the ball was batted away. It somehow landed on Tremble's arm on the way to the ground and was caught by a Broncos defender for the unlikeliest of interceptions. And it probably should have been a defensive pass interference as well.

The Panthers committed a couple of penalties to help the Broncos start their drive, and they were followed by a series of easy short to intermediate completions from Bo Nix. It was a 14 play drive and was capped off by Jonah Coleman running to the outside and stiff arming Corey Thornton to the ground on his way to a go ahead touchdown.

The offense couldn't muster a response. A run went nowhere, a pass was incomplete, then Monroe Freeling was blown by for a rapid sack to end the drive with haste.

The defense looked like they got off the field after a few plays, but Corey Thornton was called for a pass interference on third down, and it was another pretty soft call. A few plays later, Nix found Pat Bryant completely uncovered for an easy 26 yard touchdown.

Bryce Young led a march down the field. He connected with Chuba Hubbard on a fourth down slant for a clutch conversion to keep the drive alive. Things got bogged down from there, and the Panthers ended up in a 4th and 15 spot. Young found space, stepped up, and hit John Metchie down the field to pick up the first down. Young was hit in the head in the process, which added a few extra yards to put the Panthers inside the ten. On the next play, Young found McMillan open on a slant for a touchdown to make it a one score game.

The defense needed a quick stop. They stopped Jonah Coleman on first down. On second, Coleman dropped a pitch and the ball went bouncing back towards the goal line. Coleman eventually fell on it, but it was a loss of 18 yards. The Panthers made the tackle on third and long and forced the Broncos to punt coming out of the two minute warning.

Young hit McMillan on a slant for a 21 yard gain on the first play of the drive to move into the Broncos side of the field. There was an offsides Bronco, and penalty would have stopped the clock even if it was declined. Instead, the Panthers had to hurry to the line, and on the next play, Young was hit in the arm trying to throw the ball. He fumbled, and the Broncos recovered. They were able to pick up a first down to run out the clock.

The Panthers actually outplayed the Broncos on a play to play basis. They averaged 5.7 to the Broncos 4.8 yards per play. Penalties and mistakes were the difference. In the defense of the Panthers, some of the drive extending pass interference calls were very questionable. Also, the interception probably could have been a pass interference on Denver, and it was a complete fluke that the ball ended up in the hands of a Bronco.

It's a disappointing loss, but it was an admirable performance for such a banged up Panthers team against a 6-2 Broncos team. The Broncos are just a charmed team right now, and the Panthers couldn't overcome whatever black magic voodoo Sean Payton has done to earn his team some good fortune.

The Panthers travel to New Orleans to take on the Saints in a key divisional matchup.

#2757. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

#2755. Instant reaction: Broncos rally in fourth quarter to defeat Panthers in another nailbiter

The Denver Broncos battled the Carolina Panthers this afternoon in their Week 9 matchup. It was a back-and-forth game between the two teams that came down to the final of quarter of play to find a winner. In the end, the Broncos came out on top registering another comeback victory to move to 7-2 on the season. Here are some instant reactions from today's game.

For the entire first half of the season struggling on offense, the Broncos had an opportunity to shine against the Panthers. Carolina entered today's matchup sporting a bottom 5 run defense, a bad third down defense, and the second-worst red zone defense in the NFL. After scoring 10 first quarter points against the Panthers, things looked up for Denver's offense.

They dominated first half time of possession and notched 15 first downs and 159 yards of total offense. Unfortunately, a Bo Nix interception in enemy territory proved to be a big momentum change in the game. In addition to that, Denver's interior offensive line was manhandled in the first two quarters. Ben Powers and Luke Wattenberg struggled with Lee Hunter and Derrick Brown and Denver gained just 34 yards on the ground in the first half.

The Broncos' offense wasn't on the field much in the third quarter. But as usual, four quarter heroics once again came into focus. Denver was able to carve out two scoring drives. The first was a 17-play drive that went 80 yards and was capped off with a Jonah Coleman touchdown run. On their next possession, Nix was able to hit Pat Bryant on a beautiful 26-yard touchdown throw.

The touchdowns were great, but it was awesome to see Nix and the offense perform well on third down. They had a lot of big drive-sustaining conversions that made the final touchdowns possible. But that pitch to Coleman late in the game that could have cost Denver the win? Oof. That certainly raised the collective blood pressure of Broncos Country.

I was hoping for more effectiveness in the ground game, but I'm happy to see Denver's offense come together in the fourth quarter and ignite to lead the Broncos to victory. Their success was a big part of why they were able to get their fifth-straight victory of the season. Well done, offense!

The Broncos entered today's matchup with several key starters out on defense. The starting safety tandem of Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga were out, making Devon Key and J.L. Skinner the next men up. Defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike was also inactive after being placed on injured reserve.

To make things worse, Riley Moss exited the game in the second quarter after suffering a concussion. Down four starters, Bryce Young and the Panthers' offense was able to gain some steam and have success. Carolina reeled off back-to-back touchdown drives at the end of the first half and the start of the second half to take a 14 to 13 lead in the third quarter.

Whether it was the pass or the run, Vance Joseph's defense couldn't find a way to get them off the field. Young had an impressive streak of fifteen-straight completed passes. A big issue all game long was the absence of a formidable pass rush which was quite a bit of a surprise.

The Panthers entered today's matchup allowing 23 sacks. Denver wasn't able to take down Young until halfway through the four quarter when Jonathon Cooper came up big on third down and finally brought the fourth-year signal caller down.

The defense had two big plays that saved their poor play throughout the contest. The first was when Key was able to intercept a pass in the endzone that bounced off Tommy Tremble's right arm. To end the game, Nik Bonitto was able to strip sack Young in the final minutes of play to seal the deal for the Broncos.

I'll say this though, Denver giving up so many third-and-long plays, even with the injuries, was extremely concerning. I thought Joseph's conservative playcalling late in the game was perplexing. The defense will have a lot of reflection to do over the bye week to rectify some of the issues we have seen recently, but I'm happy they were able to close the game out with a big turnover.

It's incredibly hard to get a read on who this year's Broncos are. However, they just keep finding ways to win. Today's victory over the Panthers is their fifth in a row. They still maintain the AFC West lead with their victory today and hold their place as the second seed in the AFC's tough playoff race. All things considered, the bye week couldn't have come at a better time. It's time for Denver to recalibrate, regroup, and find a way to fix their issues in the second half of the season.

It is rarely pretty, but the Broncos keep finding ways to win.

The Broncos were outgained by the Panthers 353 to 303, went 2-for-4 in the red zone, including a red-zone interception. They still won their fifth consecutive game, beating Carolina 26-21 to move to 7-2. The Panthers are 3-5.

That gave Nix his 17th consecutive win in one-score games, the longest streak in the NFL since 1950.

The Panthers had 13 penalties for 119 yards, had two turnovers and Ryan Fitzgerald missed a 43-yard field goal.

Young was 28-of-39 for 276 yards with three touchdowns and an interception. Chuba Hubbard had 16 carries for 79 yards and Darren Waller had eight catches for 90 yards and a touchdown.

#2753. Giants get first win in Philadelphia since 2013

Sunday’s performance in Philadelphia wasn’t a work of art for the Giants, but it was more than good enough to end their long losing streak in the City of Brotherly Love.

Tight end Isaiah Likely’s touchdown catch in the third quarter gave the Giants their first lead since the first quarter and they expanded it to 19-11 before punting the ball back to the Eagles with 90 seconds left to play in the game. Joe Milton picked up first downs on completions to Hollywood Brown and Dallas Goedert, but rookie wideout Makai Lemon dropped a pass that would have moved them into Giants territory and running back Elijah Mitchell didn’t get out of bounds on a short catch on the next play.

Milton spiked the ball with six seconds left to play and the Eagles on their own 44-yard-line for one final heave. Milton famously uncorked a 70-yard throw at the Combine, but he never got a chance to throw the ball because he was sacked by defensive end Darius Alexander.

That was one of seven Giants sacks on the afternoon, including three from first-round pick Arvell Reese. It was Reese’s first road game against the Eagles and his 1-0 record in Philly is a big change from recent history. The Giants had lost 13 straight games in Philadelphia and the route to ending that skid featured some strange twists and turns.

Likely’s touchdown catch came on a throw from Jameis Winston, who replaced J.J. McCarthy after McCarthy hurt his hip in the third quarter. Winston played one full series and threw for 71 yards on his way to the touchdown, but McCarthy returned just before the end of the quarter and led the offense for the rest of the proceedings.

McCarthy was sacked five times, but was 12-of-19 for 127 yards when he had time to throw and he ran for 22 yards while evading pressure over the course of the afternoon. The Giants couldn’t find any other success on the ground and Sunday’s 243 yards of offense didn’t make a strong case for the Giants sitting out the trade deadline if they have a chance to acquire any kind of help for their backfield.

Wide receiver Malik Nabers had five catches for 43 yards, but dropped a pass in the end zone that would have iced the win and his body language was that of an unhappy player throughout the game. The win should make it easier to avoid it being a focal point for the team after the game, but Nabers will likely have to answer some questions about what was bugging him.

They’ll be back on the field Thursday night against the Commanders and another win would move them to 6-2-1 with a 3-0-1 record in the division. That would make them even heavier favorites to win an NFC East that is theirs for the taking.

The Eagles spent a lot of time in that position in recent years, but injuries have gutted the roster and Milton didn’t provide any significant upgrade on the offensive production that the team got with Tanner McKee at quarterback. The Eagles will have a bye week to determine which way they want to go in the future, but the 2-7 team should really only have eyes on 2027 at this point.

#2752. Knicks Week Preview: Nov. 8-14, 2026

The Knicks have bobbed over .500 for the first time this season, thanks to yesterday's return to form against the Cleveland Cavaliers. Over the upcoming week, our heroes will get a second whack at the Ohio Players, plus two beatable opponents. Let's take a peek at the schedule, shall we?

Brunson scored 31 in the first tilt, Karl-Anthony Towns added 29 points and 13 rebounds, and New York led by 19 in the third. Donovan Mitchell found his way to 37, fighting to the end; James Harden died of old age; and Evan Mobley melted into a sweaty puddle under the rim.

Cleveland might have been fatigued on Saturday (playing a SEGABABA), and coach Kenny Atkinson will surely try to mix things up in their rematch. We're curious to see what adjustments are up his sleeve. Jarrett Allen might return from the injured list, so maybe he can keep up with KAT better than Mopey Mobs?

The Knicks finish the week in Indiana. The poor Pacers can make a mess of things if you give them the ball and a head start. The Pacers can still score in a hurry, especially if you help them with turnovers and lost rebounds. Without Haliburton, Pascal Siakam and Andrew Nembhard have carried the load. #2747. Knicks Bulletin: ‘I wasn’t lying in that sense’

The Cavaliers beat the Knicks on Saturday, adding another win to their analytical spreadsheet.

Cleveland remains undefeated on that front, while New York keeps stacking dubs on the court.

On giving Landry Shamet more leeway than younger reserves and keeping bench minutes competitive:

"Obviously, you looking at a guy like Landry, he may have a little bit more leash than Pac [Dadiet]. Landry's as close to being a starter as you can imagine for us. Everybody else, they have to play and even the starters and Landry, they do, too."

On Landry Shamet's standing in the Knicks' rotation:

"About as close to being a starter as you can imagine for us."

On choosing Tyler Kolek over Jose Alvarado as the backup point guard:

"But you know, Jose had the first opportunity [against the Nets) and then I gave Tyler an opportunity in the second half and Tyler played well. So I go with Tyler and if I feel I need to make a change, Tyler's not getting it done in my eyes, I'll go back to Jose."

On Josh Hart's ability to contribute without having plays called for him:

"Josh is a connector. I don't think we call a single play for him at any time, he just goes and gets it done.

"He rebounds. Our pick and roll defense has been bad, and he's helped clean it up at times by putting him on the ball. So his versatility defensively is a bonus for us. So he's definitely going to be missed."

On facing Cleveland again after defeating the Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals:

"I mean, they're a great team. We saw them in the Eastern Conference finals. Obviously, they have another year under their belt with each other, more experience. And we saw what experience does for teams, especially like us."

On acknowledging that he underestimated Taylor Swift's history as a Knicks fan:

"Obviously with everything (going on), people have been going back and sending me all the stuff about her going to the games. And she was actually wearing a 13 jersey (in one picture). Probably Joakim Noah back in the day with Carmelo (Anthony). So, I wasn't up to date on my Taylor Swift Knicks fandom, so that's on me."

On the reaction to his comments about Taylor Swift and admitting he answered the question poorly:

"(The video) was everywhere. Everybody saw it. But it is what it is. For me, it's just a question that was asked to me that maybe I answered in the wrong way. I take that on the chin. But I love her music. We were just playing it five minutes ago and I'm singing every word to every song. Nothing against her at all."

On being a Taylor Swift fan despite questioning her Knicks fandom:

"I love her music. I probably know more songs than anybody else in the locker room. I just misspoke."

On returning to Cleveland and remembering the Knicks' championship run:

"It's human nature, you're gonna revert back and think back to the last time you were in the building. I had a quick little firing of that walking in for shootaround, but I think the general sense was that was last year. That was great. You can have those memories and hang on to that as long as we want, but ultimately this year is a new year and a new endeavor."

On the benefits of roster continuity and familiarity with Mike Brown:

"The biggest thing is just being comfortable with the guys on the floor, second year with [head coach] Mike [Brown]. I think that just breeds confidence. Familiarity breeds confidence. There's no denying that. It allows you to get to the point of conversations quicker. It makes for a good formula to find success."

On comparing his unpredictable Knicks role to that of a baseball relief pitcher:

"Especially with [my] role, I think I take a lot from my buddy Ashby, bullpen guy, you don't know when you're gonna get thrown in, what the situation's gonna be. My job might look a little different from night to night. If I'm changing my approach every night, that's not setting myself up for a good situation.

"I think in the past in my career when I was younger I would try to overcomplicate things and think I have to reinvent the wheel. I try to just keep it as simple as possible, reduce it down to my job, my impact and just play my game."

On Cleveland's Saturday loss to the Knicks:

"No excuse. These are games that we feel like we should win. We got another tough stretch coming up so there's no reason to sit here and feel bad and nothing's won in the first 10 games."

"I think we just gave them too many second-chance opportunities. Then it's too late, you're down 20 trying to fight back, but it's too late."

On the Cavaliers failing to match the Knicks' intensity:

"Got to bring your A game and we just didn't do that tonight."

On Cleveland continuing to compete despite trailing New York by 18 points:

"We could have folded down 18, could have packed it in on a back-to-back, tough week, but we kept at it."

On acknowledging that the Knicks dominated the Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals and then won the championship:

"They dominated it, and they did it again against San Antonio [in the Finals]. Analytically … there's an 'expected score,' and we've won two out of the three games.

"I think when you look back on it and take the context of the question, I'm not sure that was taken into account, which I know was a little bit of a lesson for me — like, you can just take a sound bite (and run with it).

"I would just say there was no coach more complimentary of the Knicks and honest about our performance and how they dominated us. So you live and learn a little bit with those things. But like I said, 99 percent of my comments were how they dominated us. They were by far the better team. I answered the question, as it was taken, (which was) 'And you're down 3-0, what hope do you have of even giving to your guys?'

"We get a lot of information … and I wasn't lying in that sense, but in no sense was it like, 'Oh, man, we deserve to be winning.' Like zero — zero — thought of that."

On why analytics could not outweigh the Knicks' physical and mental dominance:

"We get information that checks our process. All that being said, we were still dominated. It kind of doesn't matter (what the analytics say) because there is more than that. There is the mental toughness, the physical toughness, the flow to the game, how aggressive you are. There are all these other intangibles that go with that."

On recognizing that the Knicks earned their championship:

"They deserved it, and they did it again against San Antonio. Just an incredible, incredible run."

#2746. Puka Nacua, Myles Garrett lead Rams to 20-13 win over Commanders

LANDOVER, Md. (AP) — Matt Stafford found star receiver Puka Nacua early and often, Myles Garrett had three sacks and a forced fumble in his return and the Los Angeles Rams held on for their third straight victory, 20-13 over the Washington Commanders on Sunday.

Seemingly open all afternoon, Nacua was targeted 19 times by Stafford and finished with 14 catches for 150 yards and a touchdown as the Rams (5-4) moved above .500 for the first time this season. Stafford threw for 219 yards with an interception on 26-of-43 passing.

Nacua made a leaping, contested catch in the corner of the end zone for a 7-yard touchdown that broke a 13-all tie early in the fourth quarter.

Garrett gave a lift to the Rams' defense in his first action since Los Angeles' season-opening loss to the 49ers in Australia. The All-Pro defensive end had missed seven games with a knee injury.

Jayden Daniels went 21 of 28 for 204 yards and a touchdown and had 15 yards rushing for the Commanders (2-5-1), who couldn't generate enough offense to keep up with the Rams. Absent Treylon Burks, and with top wideout Terry McLaurin out for the season, the Commanders' passing game was inconsistent.

Two Washington drives in the final minutes ended without points, including a lateral play as time expired.

After a sluggish first half, the Rams' offense began to move the ball more consistently. Nacua was a large part of that resurgence.

The Commanders took a 10-6 lead into halftime with a defensive stand to force a Rams field goal as time expired. Van Jefferson caught a 7-yard touchdown pass from Daniels early in the second quarter for the only touchdown of the first half.

Garrett and the Rams' defense locked down after that. Despite being down two cornerbacks, the Rams forced either a punt or a turnover on five straight Commanders drives. Washington ended that scoreless stretch thanks to Nick Cross' interception of Stafford; the Commanders gained only 9 yards on four plays and kicked a field goal.

That was Washington's only score in the final 44 minutes.

Garrett, acquired from Cleveland in the offseason in a deal that helped make the Rams a preseason Super Bowl favorite had a strip-sack of Daniels — his first sack as a Ram — late in the first half to set up Brandon McManus' short field goal. That followed a fumble by Nacua that gave Washington the ball.

Rams: Guard Steve Avila left with a hamstring injury and did not return.

Commanders: Guard Lucas Patrick was ruled out with a concussion. Cornerback Amik Robertson was injured midway through the fourth quarter and did not return.

Commanders: At the New York Giants on Thursday night.

#2745. Broncos DB Devon Key awarded wild interception in the Panthers' end zone after Denver challenge

In Sunday's matchup between the Carolina Panthers and Denver Broncos, a dropped touchdown pass turned into an unbelievable interception thanks to a well-timed challenge, a key play in Denver's tight road victory.

Toward the end of the third quarter, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young threw a pass to tight end Tommy Tremble in the end zone. Though the ball ended up in the hands of Broncos defensive back Devon Key, it looked like it hit the ground first, leading officials to rule the play incomplete.

Denver used its challenge flag, leading to a review that proved successful for the Broncos. As Tremble went down while trying to make the catch, the ball rolled off his wrist before bouncing off his hand, with Key in just the right position to pluck it out of the air. It never actually hit the ground, leading officials to overturn the call and rule it a Denver pick.

Devon Key somehow got the interception in the Panthers end zone.

Because the play was ruled dead, Key did not get a chance to make a return, but the Broncos were given a touchback. Quarterback Bo Nix then led the team down the field on a 14-play, 80-yard touchdown drive to take a 19-15 lead, after Denver's 2-point conversion attempt was unsuccessful.

The game stayed tight until the end. Though the Broncos scored another fourth-quarter touchdown shortly afterward, the Panthers came back with Young finding Tetairoa McMillan in the end zone on the next drive.

A three-and-out Denver drive gave Carolina a late chance for a go-ahead touchdown, but Nik Bonitto forced Young's second turnover of Sunday with a sack and fumble recovery. The Broncos (7-2) then rode out the final minute and change for a 26-21 win.

#2744. Burkardt saves the day for Frankfurt in Paderborn as penalty king Atubolu delivers in different way

Adi Hütter surprisingly left Germany international Younes Ebnoutalib on the bench, but fellow striker Jonathan Burkardt gave them an early lead at the midpoint of a lively first-half. Ritsu Doan and Lillian Brassier had the game's first chances inside the first ten minutes.

Noah Atubolu's first save arrived minutes later as he parried away Gabriel Vidovic's curling effort. Against the run of play, the visitors took the lead as Fares Chaïbi punished Paderborn's disorganized defense with a brilliant assist for Burkardt.

After his assist to Obermair's goal, Ruben Müller nearly scored early after the restart before another decent chance for US midfielder Santiago Castaneda. Chaïbi also had a chance for his second direct goal involvement inside the lively ten minutes right after the half-time break.

With 25 minutes left to play, both coaches already made seven substitutions in total. 16-year-old midfielder Niko Ilicevic entered the scene for his second Bundesliga appearance, but Paderborn took the lead for the first time after he was dispossessed in the danger zone.

Brassier had a difficult game, and he committed a foul on substitute Marvin Pieringer inside the box. Atubolu, who saved all the previous six penalty-kicks he has faced at Freiburg and Frankfurt, dived the right way, but he wasn't able to deny Pieringer his first Paderborn goal.

Frankfurt's hopes of getting back to the game faced a huge blow a couple of minutes later as Elias Baum saw his second yellow card. Ralf Kettemann subbed off half-time substitute Deniz Zeitler in fear of a similar outcome, but the hosts failed to hold on to their slender lead.

Atubolu's penalty-kick record came to an end, but he guided Chaïbi's corner-kick to Burkardt's direction as the striker leveled the score with an unorthodox finish in the last action of the game.

#2743. Highlights: Spurs third-quarter barrage blows out Trail Blazers

Coming off an opening NBA Cup win against the Sacramento Kings, the Spurs faced a SEGABABA against the Portland Trail Blazers. After a sluggish first quarter, the Spurs, behind by 42 points in the second quarter, built their two-point lead to 15 at halftime. In the third, the Spurs drove the nail in the coffin, outscoring the Blazers 45-27 and ballooning their lead to 33 heading into the fourth. The Blazers simply could not stop the ball movement and three-point barrage by the silver and black, as the Spurs ultimately won 125-103.

Victor Wembanyama continues his early MVP campaign with another efficient high-scoring game of 29 points (9-13 FG, 3-6 3PT, 8-9 FT), seven rebounds, three assists, a block, and a steal. Despite only playing 24 minutes and not being as big a focal point of the offense as he was against Dallas and Sacramento, Wemby once again demonstrated how unguardable he truly is. After starting the season shooting under 30% from three, Wemby is now shooting 7-12 (58%) from three in his last two games.

Since he's shown he can shoot threes, Donovan Clingan steps out to guard him but immediately gets beat by Wemby on the drive to the basket. All Toumani Camara can do is go straight up, but against a seven-foot-four (he's definitely taller) alien, it's almost pointless.

The bulk of Wemby's scoring comes from inside the paint. He is dunking the ball more than any other player in the league and is even leading other TEAMS in total dunks. Where do most of his dunks come from? Lobs, of course.

The most unguardable lob threat in the league, all his teammates have to do is just throw it up above the rim to where only Wemby can grab it. Sometimes, defenders are in the way. This time, Clingan was unfortunately one of his victims.

Devin Vassell dropped another solid game with 15 points, three assists, two rebounds, and two steals. His defense somehow outshone his shooting from three. His agility and lateral movement allow him to stay in front of multiple guards and forwards. He also deflected multiple passes, and one of them turned into a steal and layup all by himself.

Stephon Castle dropped 14 points, seven rebounds, five assists, and a block. Castle, like Vassell, played like a Swiss Army knife against the Blazers. He crashed the glass, dished out dimes, and had himself some highlight buckets. The hustle play of the game was him somehow tight-roping the sideline and dishing out to an open Vassell for the corner three.

Poor Clingan. De'Aaron Fox and Castle run a beautiful DHO that results in a posterizing alley-oop with Castle dunking on his former college teammate.

Although they didn't shoot 50% from three this game, they still drained 17 compared to Portland's nine. For most Spurs fans, that third-quarter explosion showed that when everyone is bought in and focused within the flow of the offense, this team can put teams away early. The communication also reached the defense, as they held the Blazers to 76 points after 36 minutes (before garbage time). Next week, the Spurs face the Suns, Bulls, Warriors, & Jazz.

#2742. Giants QB J.J. McCarthy returns to win over Eagles after apparent hip injury after taking shot to his side

New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy briefly left Sunday's 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles early with an apparent hip injury after he took a direct shot to his side.

McCarthy, however, returned two drives later at Lincoln Financial Field and appeared to avoid any major injury.

McCarthy, on New York's second play of the third quarter, scrambled for a few yards up the left side. As he went down, McCarthy turned and lowered his right shoulder, which was drilled hard by Eagles linebacker Zack Baun.

McCarthy was quickly replaced by backup Jameis Winston, and went over to the sideline.

McCarthy threw the ball on the sideline, but he was in so much pain and actually dropped down to the ground after screaming out while reaching for his side. He slammed his helmet down to the bench out of frustration.

McCarthy eventually jogged off to the locker room. The Giants said he was questionable to return with a hip injury.

McCarthy went 9-of-13 passing for 101 yards before he went down. The Giants entered halftime trailing by two points after they kicked a pair of field goals in the first quarter. Saquon Barkley found the end zone for the Eagles on a 3-yard run early, and the Eagles completed the 2-point conversion.

While Winston initially struggled, he mounted a 14-play, 76-yard touchdown drive on his second time out on Sunday afternoon to put the Giants ahead. He capped that with a 5-yard toss to Isaiah Likely, which gave New York a 13-8 lead.

McCarthy returned for the Giants' next drive, and seemed back to his old self. Any significant hip injury, it seems, has been avoided.

McCarthy got his NFL start with the Minnesota Vikings, but he ended up getting only 10 starts with the franchise before Minnesota traded him to New York in September. Sunday's outing was only his second start since taking over for Winston, who was in for the already injured Jaxson Dart.

The Giants kicked two more field goals the rest of the way to secure the eight-point win, which pushed them to 5-2-1 on the season and kept their lead in the NFC East intact. McCarthy ended up with 127 passing yards, but did not throw a touchdown in the contest. Winston went 6-of-8 for 71 yards and a touchdown.

#2741. Palace consider replacing Sage, with Frank among contenders

Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage is in serious danger of losing his job only five months into his reign, with the club bottom of the Premier League going into the international break.

Sunday's 3-1 defeat by Liverpool was Palace's fourth successive league loss, with Sage's side having won just two of their 10 league matches this season.

The club have held internal talks aimed at deciding Sage's future and his potential successor.

Former Tottenham and Brentford manager Thomas Frank is viewed as a strong candidate, while ex-Nottingham Forest boss Sean Dyche also has some support internally.

Both are out of work and would be available to start immediately.

Palace have taken just seven points from their 10 league matches and have the worst defensive record in the league, having conceded 24 goals.

They are also 21st in the Europa League, currently enough for a play-off spot, with only one win from their four matches.

If he is dismissed, Frenchman Sage could become the first managerial casualty of the Premier League season.

He was appointed on a three-year contract in June after Oliver Glasner departed at the end of last season.

"It's not from the dream to the nightmare," the 47-year-old said after the defeat by Liverpool.

"I'm not feeling this. I'm just in my job, and focusing on my job, and what I have to do to find the solution.

"The results are not at this level, and I know I have to push more on those things, especially in our way of playing, to make that move."

Sage previously led Lens to a second-place finish in Ligue 1 and a first French Cup triumph in their 120-year history.

However, he has been unable to replicate Glasner's success at Palace. Glasner, who now manages Nottingham Forest, led Palace to a first FA Cup title and a Europa Conference League triumph.

Palace are winless in the league since 11 October, with their losing run sparked by a 5-0 loss to fierce rivals Brighton.

After that match, Sage said he felt "shame" and admitted he did not know if he would be given time to turn Palace's fortunes around.

However, there was a degree of sympathy from some behind the scenes.

Injuries were not kind to his plans, while the absence of Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr - due to a mixture of fitness and personal issues, related to both players' desire to leave the club - did not help the start of his reign.

However, three more league defeats have followed, with Palace hitting the bar and having a goal ruled out in their loss to Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

"We have to be more competitive," Sage said on Sunday.

"At the moment, we create some things, we expect a lot of things, but we don't have the results expected."

Palace's next Premier League match is at Coventry on 21 November following the two-week international break.

#2740. Pistons vs Lakers preview: Best Defense vs best offense

Does it get any better than the No. 1 offense versus the No. 1 defense? The Detroit Pistons find themselves in that matchup as the 122-point-per-game Los Angeles Lakers visit Motown tonight.

Luka Dončić and the Lakers put up plenty of buckets, but scoring on Detroit is still an impossible task. The Pistons only surrender 101 points a game. Smothering defense every night.

Detroit's defense has its biggest test of the season if Dončić suits up this evening. He's questionable with lower back tightness.

It would be a shame if we're robbed of Cade Cunningham going head-to-head with another MVP candidate. The bigger shame would be if we miss out on Dončić versus Ausar Thompson. That matchup is like Jerry Rice versus Deion Sanders with how both are operating.

Detroit hasn't played since Wednesday's loss to the Philadelphia 76ers. They've had plenty of time to rest up. They'll need it if Dončić suits up.

Dončić is averaging 40 points. He's shooting 42% on nearly 14 3s a game. He gets to the line more than anybody. It's basically no stopping Dončić at the moment. This is a Wilt Chamberlain-like hot streak. Those two are the only players to average 40 nine games into the season. Whew, to say he's balling is an understatement.

But tasks like this are why the Pistons employ Ausar Thompson. If *anybody* can slow Dončić down, it's the best perimeter defender on the planet. Dončić usually has success against quick defenders with wiry strength, but Ausar is bigger and stronger this season. We'll be keeping tabs on how Ausar takes Dončić's bumps tonight. Ausar has the quick hands to disrupt things as well.

This might be a game where we see Paul Reed getting to the level and blitzing a bunch. J.B. Bickerstaff may decide to get the ball out of Dončić's hands and force someone else to beat them. Reed is capable of coming to the level on screens and muddying things up.

I'm sure Dončić will see some Cade tonight too. Cade won't make it easy with his sturdy frame. On the other end, the Lakers only have a few perimeter defenders to throw at Cade.

Matisse Thybulle is firmly in LA's rotation as he's started all 10 games. He's still a defensive playmaking threat. Cade deals with defenders like this nightly, but Thybulle is a plus defender nonetheless. So is Ziaire Williams. The springy 25-year-old treats every possession as if he'll never get in the game again if he doesn't go hard.

Those two are solid defensively, and Jake LaRavia competes. Outside of that, Detroit will have plenty of favorable matchups (Walker Kessler is a great rim protector and is off to a good offensive start. He can make a difference).

Dončić displays effort and is trying to shake the terrible defender narrative on his name, but attacking him is still the best way to slow him down. Make him work and keep him involved in actions.

Austin Reaves falls into the same boat. He's under Dončić on the Lakers' best defenders on the team list. Anybody with that matchup should look to be aggressive.

Reaves spends most of his time covering shooting guards. Will JJ Redick make Reaves chase Duncan Robinson all night? That's probably not ideal. Robinson runs even great defenders into the ground.

Robinson's light-em-up stretch continues as he's fourth in 3s made (35). Only Dončić, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, and Steph Curry have made more.

Detroit is letting it fly from deep as a team. According to Cleaning the Glass, 40 percent of their shots are coming from 3 (15th) compared to 31 percent last year (29th). Their rim rate has flipped the other way, but getting Jalen Duren back should rectify that.

The best offense versus the best defense is a mandatory viewing appointment. Can Ausar slow down the MVP-favorite? Do the Pistons show why they're an elite defense and smother Dončić as a team? Does Cade deliver a masterclass against a guy he'll be compared to for the foreseeable future if he's in the MVP race? We'll find out at 6 PM. Be there!

Detroit Pistons (6-2): Cade Cunningham, Duncan Robinson, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

Los Angeles Lakers (8-2): Luka Dončić, Austin Reaves, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia, Walker Kessler

#2738. Winston, McCarthy combine to lead Giants to 19-11 win and hand Eagles 7th straight loss

PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Jameis Winston replaced the injured J.J. McCarthy long enough to throw a go-ahead touchdown pass and help the New York Giants keep their grip on the NFC East and beat Philadelphia 19-11 on Sunday to hand the Eagles their seventh straight loss.

The Eagles (2-7) are on their longest losing streak since they lost eight straight games in Andy Reid's final season in 2012.

With Jalen Hurts likely out for the season with blood clots and a playoff berth all but gone, the Eagles could get a roster makeover at Tuesday's NFL trade deadline.

The Giants (5-2-1) are the only team in the division with a winning record.

The Eagles had beaten the Giants 13 straight times at home — including one playoff win — since New York last won on Oct. 27, 2013.

It doesn't seem to matter who's playing quarterback for the Giants.

McCarthy suffered a hip injury in the third quarter that briefly forced him out of the game and the Giants trailing 8-6.

Coach John Harbaugh turned to Winston — who held the starting job for four games after No. 1 QB Jaxson Dart was injured — to rally New York.

Winston did enough in his cameo to keep New York's first division title since 2011 within reach. He hit wide receiver Malachi Fields for 14 yards that took the ball to the Eagles 3-yard line and followed two plays later with a 5-yard TD pass to Isaiah Likely that sent the Giants into the fourth quarter with a 13.-8 lead.

McCarthy returned for the final play of the third quarter. He completed 12 of 19 passes for 127 yards and no touchdowns or interceptions. Winston was 6 of 8 for 71 yards and the lone touchdown.

Dominic Zvada kicked field goals of 53 and 49 yards for a 6-0 lead in the first quarter and connected from 38 and 49 yards in the second half for a 19-8 lead.

Like the Giants, the Eagles have also cycled through quarterbacks because of injuries and ineffectiveness.

Tanner McKee went 0-3 since taking over for Hurts as the starter before he was benched this week for Joe Milton.

The 26-year-old Milton had appeared in five NFL games in relief and was suddenly tasked with saving the Eagles' season.

He showed flashes of the speed and strong arm that McKee doesn't have. Like McKee. Milton couldn't do much to move the offense.

Saquon Barkley scored on a 3-yard run late in the first quarter and — after a Giants penalty on the extra point — Milton ran in for the 2-point conversion for an 8-7 lead. Milton punctuated the score with a backflip in the end zone that got a rise out of the crowd.

Milton went 18 of 34 for 169 yards and was sacked on the final play of the game. Jake Elliott added a 45-yard field goal.

Jonathan Greenard finally got his first sack as an Eagle after he was acquired from Minnesota in a draft-weekend trade. The edge rusher subsequently agreed to a four-year, $98 million extension, including $50 million guaranteed.

Braden Mann unleashed an 86-yard punt for the Eagles at the end of the first half. It was the longest punt in the NFL since 2001. Mann punted out of the end zone (the ball was spotted at the Eagles 8) and rolled out of bounds at the Giants 6-yard line.

Mann followed with a 60-yarder to end the Eagles' first drive of the second half. He also lost 2 yards on a botched punt.

Former Eagles quarterback Randall Cunningham actually holds the franchise record with a 91-yarder in 1989.

Eagles head into a bye and return on Nov. 22 to host the Steelers.

#2737. Eagles-Giants instant analysis: Quarterback change cannot fix offense

The Eagles changed the quarterback without changing the central problem. Their offense still could not produce enough consistent gains to support a defense that gave them a legitimate chance to win.

Sunday's 19-11 loss to the Giants pushed Philadelphia to 2-7, extending a losing streak that has swallowed a 2-0 start. Joe Milton supplied movement, a few extended plays and an early celebration, but the Eagles finished with 220 yards and one touchdown. The evidence pointed toward problems that reach beyond the player taking the snap.

Milton rushed for 64 yards on nine attempts, accounting for most of Philadelphia's 92 rushing yards. His 19-yard first-half scramble extended the touchdown drive, and his mobility created gains that weren't available within the original structure of several plays.

That contribution mattered. It also exposed how little the conventional offense generated. Saquon Barkley and Elijah Mitchell combined for 28 yards on 16 carries, leaving Milton to create too much of the rushing production himself.

New York collected seven sacks and 11 quarterback hits, with Arvell Reese responsible for three sacks and a forced fumble. Philadelphia lost 41 yards on sacks, reducing Milton's 169 passing yards to 128 net passing yards.

Those losses repeatedly turned difficult possessions into nearly impossible ones. The Eagles need to evaluate protection assignments, individual execution, and the quarterback's responses together. Assigning every sack to one cause would miss the larger breakdown.

Philadelphia held New York to 243 yards and 2.6 yards per rushing attempt while collecting six sacks. The Giants' starting running back, Devin Singletary, needed 21 carries to gain 31 yards.

The defense was not flawless. Winston's touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely exposed a damaging red-zone coverage breakdown. Still, allowing 19 points while generating that much disruption should have given Philadelphia a workable path.

The Eagles scored eight points in the first quarter and three over the final three periods. They converted five of 18 third downs and failed twice on fourth down.

Milton's athleticism gives the coaching staff something to develop. That doesn't excuse an offense that cannot consistently protect, run, or stay ahead of the chains. Philadelphia needs a plan that creates repeatable gains instead of depending on its quarterback to rescue broken possessions.

This article originally appeared on Eagles Wire: Eagles-Giants instant analysis: Quarterback change cannot fix offense

#2735. What we learned from the Spurs’ win over the Trail Blazers

If you've been looking for a signature San Antonio Spurs win early in the 2026-27 season, look no further. On the second game of a back-to-back, the Spurs waltzed into enemy territory and blew out a team motivated to get revenge. It was one of the first times we've seen this year's Spurs put it all together against a playoff-caliber team.

Defense was the name of the game in San Antonio's 125-103 win over the Portland Trail Blazers. Both teams played incredibly physical (or just flopped a lot). But the Spurs were the enforcers overall. Stephon Castle set the tone on the perimeter with some suffocating defense on two of the Blazers' best players, Deni Advija and Jrue Holiday. Advija was particularly frustrated by Castle's defense, scoring just 15 points on 5-13 shooting.

The rest of the team forced turnovers. Portland coughed it up 18 times, leading to 23 easy points for the Spurs. The tape will show that the Spurs dominated this game with force and athleticism. The stat sheet shows they won a lot of the hustle stats, too. San Antonio won the rebounding battle by 13 and grabbed 14 offensive boards. The force they showed against Portland is the same as what they showed last season in their NBA Finals run, but more refined.

The Blazers just feel like a team the Spurs will have to beat in the Victor Wembanyama era. They are young (for the most part), tough, and skilled. Beating them down in such a dominant fashion after the playoff victory last season is a clear sign that San Antonio has not taken a step back, despite some bumps to start the season. It also showed a lot of grit and edge from the Spurs. It was exactly the type of victory this team needed early in the season.

I gave the second unit a tough time in the last WWL. They were MUCH better against Portland. Luke Kornet in particular had one of his best games of the season with 6 points, 4 rebounds, 2 assists, and a block. There were fewer moments when Kornet needed to go one-on-one with a driver at the rim, as the perimeter defense made it harder for the Blazers to get clear drives to the basket. What was even more impressive about Kornet's game is that he actually took a few shots when he was open. Typically, the backup center isn't even thinking about shooting, but he hit a pop-a-shot early in the game and took a jumper from the free-throw line that didn't fall. Just getting Kornet to take those kinds of shots when they are available will help the second-unit offense tremendously.

It's been a minute since we got a sub-25-minute elite performance from Wembanyama. Not because the performances haven't been elite, but because he's usually playing more than 25 minutes. He had 29 points on 9-for-13 shooting, including three triples. Portland had absolutely no answer for the early-season MVP candidate. In the last two games, he's become more selective with his jump shots, and the results have been better looks that are going in more often.

Carter Bryant got an opportunity to play early in the game and made the most of it. He hit a pair of three-pointers, got a deflection and a block, providing energy off the bench. Bryant still struggles with overaggressiveness on defense. He picked up 5 fouls in just 17 minutes on Saturday. Bryant has a lot of talent; it just needs to be harnessed with improved awareness and experience.

The Blazers continued their strategy of guarding Castle with Donovan Clingan and putting Toumani Camara on Wembanyama. It's safe to say the Spurs have figured out how to defeat that coverage. It helps that Castle made two of his five three-pointers, and Wembanyama is a game-breaker. Portland still needed to send doubles at Wembanyama, and when they did, the Spurs were able to get easy looks when the ball was passed out.

#2734. What did we learn from Shedeur Sanders' start vs. Saints? Instant reaction

NEW ORLEANS ― The Browns won a game where the quarterback spent most of it struggling to find consistency. Then, in the fourth quarter, found a way to make a play.

That had been the wasy Deshaun Watson had been quarterbacking the Browns to five wins in their first eight games. However, with Watson inactive as he returned from a concussion, Shedeur Sanders made his first start of the season at the New Orleans Saints.

However, for most of the game, the story of the game was both teams' inability to turn opportunities into touchdowns. They came alive in the final six minutes of regulation and then into overtime for what ended up being a 23-22 overtime loss to the Saints.

The first of four touchdowns and one field goal in the final six minutes came when Sanders hit wide receiver KC Concepcion for a 62-yard touchdown with 5:41 remaining. That was one of two 60-plus-yard completions for Sanders, who also had a 60-yarder to Denzel Boston that ultimately only netted a field goal.

Sanders also had a great throw to Jerry Jeudy on the drive that ended with Andre Szmyt's overtime-forcing 51-yard field goal with eight seconds left in regulation. That was one of three regulation field goals for Szmyt.

The Saints, though, scored touchdowns on their last true regulation possession and only overtime possession. The Browns scored on Harold Fannin Jr.'s wild 39-yard catch-and-run in overtime, but couldn't convert what would've been the game-winning two-point converion.

Here are our instant thoughts and reactions immediately after the clock hit all zeros.

Sanders, for the first three quarters, played like a backup quarterback who received practice reps for three days and then had a walkthrough the day before the game. Which isn't so much a shot as it is a reality for a backup.

Then the fourth quarter and overtime happened and he came alive. He finished 19-of-31 for 297 yards with two touchdowns, after starting 7-of-12 for 100 yards over the first three quarters.

The second-year pro seemed, at times, a tad tentative as he was catching back up to the speed of a real game. That's not to say that there weren't moments, but there was never a sense of any consistency in the play.

Take the Browns' two trips inside the Saints 10, one on each side of halftime. Both times they got there, Sanders immediately got sacked to set them back.

The first one ended with a fourth-down stop by the Saints. The second one, set up by a big throw to Denzel Boston for 60 yards ended with an Andre Szmyt field goal.

The Browns had penalties in all three phases by the time each of them had had a chance to be on the field. They had penalties in all four quarters, with all three phases contributing to the issue.

By the end of the game, the Browns had nine penalties for 53 yards. They had allowed New Orleans to get two first downs because of them.

More than anything, they just continue to show a lack of discipline that still exists. They lead the NFL in penalties, which is unacceptable for any team.

The biggest catch of the game for the Browns may have been the one Jerry Jeudy made on the Browns sideline with former Browns cornerback M.J. Emerson in tight coverage. It was a 30-yarder that put Cleveland at the Saints 40.

That eventually led to the Szmyt game-tying 51-yard field goal with eight seconds remaining. Meaning, Jeudy once again had one of his few catches keep a critical drive going.

Jeudy had three combined catches between the home wins over the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Baltimore Ravens that help on key game-winning drive. This one wasn't on a winning drive, but the Browns avoided a regulation loss because of it.

The Browns allowed the Saints to move the ball at will throughout the game. Yet another terrible run game ran all over them, while a mid passing game suddenly was prolific.

The Saints needed a touchdown with less than two minutes left? Effortless. They needed to take the opening kick of overtime and move it down the field? Not a problem.

The Browns defense had its share of plays over the course of the afternoon. That's why New Orleans only had one regulation touchdown.

However, they weren't able to make a bad offense look bad. Instead, much like the Tennessee Titans, they looked as good as they have all season.

#2733. Dan Campbell explains decision to bench Christian Mahogany

The Detroit Lions made a very surprising personnel decision in their 19-9 win over the Miami Dolphins. Lions coach Dan Campbell decided to give Miles Frazier his first career start at left guard over Christian Mahogany. There weren't any indications that Mahogany's play had dipped—in fact, he was nationally praised for his performance against the Vikings—so his benching came as a complete surprise.

After the Lions' win, Campbell explained the decision, noting it was a disciplinary action.

"That was team rules (for) Mahogany. It was really that simple," Campbell said. "Miles deserved his opportunity, so he got it. Doesn't mean it stays that way, but that was the way it was going to be today."

In his first career start, Frazier clearly struggled in the first half, giving up several early pressures to Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler. He did settle down in the second half, though, helping the Lions score on every second-half possession—outside of the last drive that bled the remainder of the clock.

Still, there will be plenty of questions going forward about what exactly Mahogany did to earn a benching. Not only was he getting national praise and passing the eye test, but he has earned PFF's 10th-highest grade among guards with at least 130 snaps.

Hopefully, he can get back in the Lions' good graces and continue his strong season.

#2730. Chase Briscoe’s 2026 NASCAR Season Ends in Heartbreak After Engine Failure at Homestead

Chase Briscoe's hopes of ending the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series season on a high note came to a sudden, devastating end Sunday at Homestead-Miami Speedway.

The Joe Gibbs Racing driver was running competitively in the season finale when his No. 19 Toyota suffered an engine failure late in Stage 1. Smoke poured from the car as Briscoe slowed on the track, bringing out the caution and ultimately ending the opening stage under yellow.

There would be no recovery for Briscoe, whose afternoon ended after just 78 laps of the scheduled 267-lap race.

The mechanical failure also had major championship implications. With Briscoe eliminated from contention, Kyle Larson secured the 2026 Cup Series title, even as the race itself continued.

For Briscoe, it was an especially frustrating ending considering how competitive his car had been before the failure.

Briscoe had shown promising speed throughout the opening stage, leading 33 laps and running among the frontrunners before trouble struck.

After climbing out of his Toyota, the 31-year-old made clear that the performance of the car wasn't the problem.

"No. We were really good there pace-wise," Briscoe said when asked about the failure.

He acknowledged noticing a warning sign before the engine gave way.

"A little bit of a vibration," he explained.

The failure was particularly difficult to accept because Briscoe believed he had a legitimate opportunity to compete for the victory.

"Super unfortunate. Felt like we were gonna be in the mix," he said.

Instead, his No. 19 Toyota was officially out of the race, leaving Briscoe to watch the remainder of the season finale from the sidelines.

The caution caused by his engine failure also brought Stage 1 to an early conclusion, interrupting a race that had already featured several changes for the lead.

Although Briscoe entered Sunday's finale already eliminated from championship contention, he still had plenty to race for. His No. 19 Toyota showed the speed to compete near the front, making the mechanical failure all the more frustrating.

The timing was particularly unfortunate for Joe Gibbs Racing, which still had two drivers, Denny Hamlin and Christopher Bell, mathematically capable of challenging Kyle Larson for the championship.

For Briscoe, however, the disappointment was more personal. After leading 33 laps and showing the potential to contend for the win, he was left wondering what might have been.

Despite the abrupt ending, Briscoe took a moment during his post-race interview to express his appreciation for Toyota and those who supported him throughout the season.

It wasn't the farewell to 2026 he had envisioned. Instead of fighting for a victory in the final race of the year, Briscoe was forced to watch from the sidelines as the championship battle continued without him.

#2726. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2725. Arnav’s Analysis: Takeaways From Rutgers’ 31-10 Loss At Wisconsin

After a first half in which Rutgers hung with Wisconsin, tying the score at 10 before a late Badgers field goal, the Scarlet Knights ran out of steam and did not score once in the second half. It was a stronger performance from AJ Surace, going 14-for-24 for 161 yards and a touchdown of 30 yards to Dyzier Carter, but that was not enough to overcome all the injuries, lack of scoring, and defensive struggles for the Knights.

Defensively, Rutgers held steady for the first half, but the same flaws plagued RU in the second half with wide-open scores, missed tackles, and allowing open throws for the freshman quarterback Ryan Hopkins. Antwan Raymond and Clay Thevenin were held under 100 combined yards despite carrying the football 25 times, and the offense suffered without their top lineman, quarterback, and wide receiver.

Here are my takeaways from another brutal defeat, Rutgers' seventh of this dismal season.

With the Rutgers defense largely holding Wisconsin in check other than the early touchdown, the offense was able to hold serve, and tight end Logan Blake had a nifty catch in triple coverage, having to rip the ball away from Badgers defenders for a first down. Clay Thevenin had three straight carries before Surace found Elias Coke for an 11-yard gain.

After two plays for no gain, Surace found Coke again for a seven-yard pass on third down, and Jack Scullion knocked through a 45-yard field goal to put Rutgers on the board 7-3. The offensive highlight of the day came on the next series, in which three straight run plays led to a beautiful deep ball for Dyzier Carter, who scored his first career touchdown.

However, the second half, the offense completely sputtered, as the opening drive saw a 15-yard pass to Ben Black III and ten yard pass to Dyzier Carter, but resulted in a punt despite getting across midfield. The next couple drives were worse, as the Knights gained eight yards in a three-and-out and then gaining eight net yards with one first down.

With the Badgers cruising down the field for touchdowns, Rutgers did not have the firepower to match any of the scores, and two sacks on Surace led to an incompletion intended for Black on a desparation fourth down heave.

Even a Wisconsin fumble recovered by Rutgers was not enough, as the AJ Surace-led offense was unable to generate any scoring drives or points against the staunch Badgers' front. Cooper Catalano had 14 total tackles and 2.5 per loss, while five different Badgers got home for sacks against a Rutgers offensive line missing star left guard Kwabena Asamoah and right tackle Tyler Needham.

Although at times Antwan Raymond and Clay Thevenin were able to move the ball on the ground, Raymond was limited to 56 yards on 15 carries (3.7 yards per carry), while Thevenin had 10 rushes for 40 yards (four yards per carry). Aiden Gibson and Ja'Shon Benjamin's late carries were negated by yardage lost on sacks by AJ Surace, for a team rushing total of just 94 yards. Surace was briefly replaced by Ashenfelder after an injury saw him leave the field, but he was able to quickly return to the field to finish the drive.

Through the air, Surace was sorely missing KJ Duff, as Black III led the team with six catches for 70 yards. Carter had the lone touchdown and finished with 40 yards on two catches, while Raymond added 21 yards with a reception. Elias Coke and Logan Blake rounded out the receiving column with two catches each for 18 and 14 yards respectively, while Thevenin lost two yards as the receivers were held to 161 total yards.

After both teams exchanged punts on their opening drives, Wisconsin drove down the field with the all too familiar chunk plays through the air: 15-yard pass, 9-yard pass, 18-yard run, and a 21-yard pass from Ryan Hopkins to Eugene Hilton Jr. to take an early 7-0 lead before the Scarlet Knights answered with a field goal.

The defense then held steady, allowing one field goal after a Rutgers three-and-out and punt from their own seven yard line set the Badgers up in plus territory. After the lone Knights' touchdown, they allowed another field goal, spurred by a 26-yard pass to Shamar Rigby and a pass interference on Devonte Anderson.

In the second half, it was an entirely different story, as the Rutgers offense sputtering resulted in repeated scoring drives for Wisconsin. Three separate plays went for 16 yards as the Badgers went up 16-10, then UW made Rutgers pay for a targeting call on Tariq Hayer as Hopkins connected with Ryan Schwendeman over the middle.

The game was largely decided on the next sequence with another Rutgers punt giving way to a 66-yard touchdown pass from Hopkins to tight end Jacob Harris, who ran the ball 47 yards up the right sideline while breaking and evading tackles. Rigby and Harris both crossed 70 yards in four and two plays, respectively.

For the Scarlet Knights, Zaire Angoy had a sack and 1.5 tackles for loss, while Hayer led the team in tackles with seven. Angoy and Kromah combined for a three-yard loss play on Darrion Dupree which set up a field goal, while DJ Allen had Rutgers' other sack.

The rush defense held up relatively well, holding the Badgers' run game to 122 total yards. Hilton led Wisconsin with 39 yards on three carries, while lead back Abu Sama had 35 yards on nine carries. The play of the defensive line has certainly improved, as the Badgers were held to just 4.2 yards per carry.

However, they made a true freshman quarterback making his first start look like a seasoned veteran, as Ryan Hopkins went 18-24 for 241 yards, three touchdowns, and no interceptions. Many of the throws were for over ten yards as the defensive gave up big and intermediate plays in space, as par for the course.

In total, Rutgers allowed 31 points, a near-perfect game from Hopkins, and tons of chunk plays all afternoon as Wisconsin turned a 13-10 halftime lead into a 31-10 victory to clinch bowl eligibility.

Next up for the Scarlet Knights is a Nebraska team that has watched a 5-0 start evaporate into four straight losses. After leading Indiana 17-6, the Cornhuskers fell 20-17 to the Hoosiers, then fell 17-14 at Oregon at the hands of Dylan Raiola and then a stunning defeat to Washington after leading most of the way.

Last week, Nebraska scored the opening touchdown, but the Illini scored three straight, and the Huskers were out of answers after Anthony Colandrea found Jacory Barney Jr. for a long score to cut the lead to eight. It was an upset victory for the Illini, and it sends Nebraska to New Jersey completely reeling.

However, the Scarlet Knights have looked all out of sorts, and are without Asamoah the rest of the season while Duff and Lonergan are uncertain for next week and beyond. Rutgers has never defeated Nebraska despite a few close calls, including the last two meetings which were decided by one point and one touchdown, respectively.

It will be hard to envision Rutgers finding a way to win, with the state of their offense being injured and defense struggling deeply, particularly through the air. However, the month of November continues to get easier, as the Scarlet Knights will have a chance to potentially pick off either Nebraska, Penn State, and Michigan State as the team looks to close out 2026 on a brighter note.
