#2687. Kings trade wing Nique Clifford to Thunder for two second-round picks

Second-year wing Nique Clifford was not getting much run in Sacramento, he was unimpressive in Summer League, but the real question has been: Is that because Clifford is not really an NBA player, or is it because of the Kings and coach Doug Christie's player development and usage?

The Oklahoma City Thunder are betting on the latter, as they have agreed to trade for Clifford from the Kings for two second-round picks (Utah's 2028 and Minnesota's 2030), a story broken by Shams Charania of ESPN.

The Thunder are looking for wing depth after potential season-ending injuries to Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace.

Clifford, the No. 24 pick in 2025 out of Colorado State, had largely fallen out of the Kings' rotation, and the team worked with him to find a new home, Charania reports. Clifford will make $3.3 million this season and $3.4 million next season, with a team option for nearly $6 million for 2028-29.

Clifford, a 6'5" wing, was averaging 6.3 minutes per game for the Kings, averaging 1.6 points per game on 35.3% shooting. Will putting him in the Thunder system and their development program change things for the 24-year-old? The Thunder are betting yes.

The Kings have just 13 players on the roster and have two weeks to add a 14th player to meet the league minimum.

#2686. "A huge dream": Jobe Bellingham grateful to Kovač after earning England call-up

Borussia Dortmund kept pace with Bayern Munich at the top of the Bundesliga table after overcoming Elversberg 2-1. Following the final whistle, Felix Nmecha reflected on a challenging afternoon for BVB:

"I think I struck the ball well twice today," Nmecha said with a laugh. "We knew Elversberg were a good footballing side, and they certainly didn't make things easy for us. In the end, you have to fight, that's what you have to do, and then you win."

Asked about the ongoing title battle with Bayern Munich, Nmecha played down its significance at this stage of the season.

"It's a long season, and the battle with Bayern isn't decisive for us just yet. We're taking it one game at a time. That's all we can do right now."

Meanwhile, Jobe Bellingham had plenty of reasons to celebrate following his selection for the England national team. The Dortmund midfielder credited Kovač and his coaching staff for helping him reach this milestone.

"I'm really grateful to my coach Niko Kovač. My development and the fact that I was selected for the national team are largely thanks to him and the coaching staff. I'm really happy, and I want to keep working hard and developing further," Bellingham explained.

The 20-year-old also spoke about the possibility of sharing the pitch with his brother Jude at international level – a prospect that would fulfil a childhood dream.

"Playing alongside my brother Jude for England is a huge dream. I can't stop smiling about it. We dreamed about this when we played together in the garden. I don't want to jinx anything because it hasn't happened yet, but I'm really looking forward to it, and I know he is too," he added.

#2685. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2684. Matchups that cost Colts in wild loss to Cowboys, including Sauce Gardner and Jonathan Taylor

INDIANAPOLIS — The Colts nearly pulled off an upset on Sunday.

Embattled and playing under the fires of trade speculation, Indianapolis fought its way back to take a 3-point lead late in the game ... only to have the defense give it back up, allowing a touchdown and a 27-23 Cowboys win.

Indianapolis (2-7) now turns its eyes to Tuesday's trade deadline, and how many players might be playing elsewhere next season.

Sauce Gardner is supposed to be the team's best cornerback, a shutdown player the Colts traded two first-round picks and wide receiver Adonai Mitchell to get before the deadline last season.

And he was responsible for the play that ended up costing the Colts the game on Sunday. Gardner was put in 1-on-1 coverage against Ryan Flournoy, a sixth-round pick in 2024 who is playing a critical role only because Dallas did not have George Pickens.

Gardner had already escaped a bad highlight earlier in the game, failing to get his head around to look at the ball on a throw to CeeDee Lamb that only ended up being incomplete because Lamb didn't get both feet inbounds.

The veteran cornerback's ball skills have always been questioned, and he failed to find the ball on the most important throw of the game.

After the Colts took a late 23-20 lead on a Spencer Shrader field goal, Dallas quarterback Dak Prescott went deep in 1-on-1 coverage to Flournoy.

But he never got his head around, allowing Flournoy to haul in a 46-yard pass that gave Dallas a chance to play for the game-winning touchdown instead of a game-tying field goal.

Gardner was supposed to be the "prize" of the 2025 trade deadline.

Days before the 2026 deadline, Gardner showed why he wasn't worth the price the Colts paid to get him.

Lamb is the best Dallas player, the only high-powered weapon at Dak Prescott's disposal on a day when George Pickens was not available.

Indianapolis didn't do a great job of taking away Lamb on Sunday.

But the Pro Bowl-caliber wide receiver did a decent job of limiting his own impact.

Lamb caught 10 passes for 195 yards and a touchdown, bouncing back from a slow start to seemingly break the game open on an inexplicable Indianapolis coverage bust near the end of the first half.

Veteran cornerback Charvarius Ward appeared to pass Lamb off to strong safety Hunter Wohler, who's not an excellent coverage option, and a wide-open Lamb caught a 48-yard pass for a score.

He could have turned in an even bigger day, but Lamb was flagged twice for offensive pass interference for pushing off of Colts defenders.

Then he was involved in one of the weirdest plays of the NFL season so far. Under pressure on third-and-long, Prescott flung a wounded duck in the direction of Lamb on the sideline, and the receiver made a remarkable diving catch, grabbing the ball just before it hit the turf.

Indianapolis cornerback Kenneth Harris didn't touch Lamb down, and the alert Cowboys receiver got up and took off running for a 48-yard gain.

But Lamb wasn't able to hold onto the ball at the end of the run and he fumbled the ball away to Harris, erasing the play on a weird day for the Dallas wide receiver.

Taylor, the subject of so many trade rumors for weeks, seemed to have an excellent matchup on Sunday.

Dallas entered Sunday's game with the NFL's worst rush defense, a terrible unit that ranked dead-last in the league in yards and second-to-last in yards per carry.

Indianapolis struggled to run the ball instead. Perhaps still working through the loss of Quenton Nelson, the Colts had trouble controlling the line of scrimmage, and Taylor wasn't able to find much running room. Taylor ran the ball 13 times for just 46 yards, failing to break any runs longer than seven yards.

Taylor also made the game's biggest mistake.

Driving with a chance to take the lead, Taylor got swallowed by Quinnen Williams at the line of scrimmage and lost the ball, fumbling to take away a scoring opportunity.

Backup running back Seth McGowan had the two biggest running plays of the game, scoring a touchdown and ripping off a 36-yard gain later in the game.

An Indianapolis team that has struggled all season was always going to need some help against a Cowboys team that remains full of star power.

Dallas gave it to the Colts with terrible discipline.

The Cowboys were penalized 14 times for a whopping 153 yards, routinely putting themselves behind the sticks, wiping plays off the board and giving Indianapolis a chance to stay in the game despite another ugly performance from the offense.

For the most part, none of the calls — other than the two Lamb penalties, which seemed minor — were hard to understand. Dallas simply shot itself in the foot, repeatedly, allowing the Colts to hang around as long as possible.

Joel A. Erickson and Nathan Brown cover the Coltsall season. Get more coverage on IndyStarTV and with the Colts Insider newsletter.

#2678. MLB rumors: Mets' Bo Bichette makes contract decision, familiar All-Star back on trade block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base.

For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

#2677. Joe Milton’s first Eagles start brings mobility, seven sacks and a loss

Joe Milton gave the Eagles a different look Sunday, but his first start in Philadelphia ended with a familiar result. The Giants won 19-11 at Lincoln Financial Field as Milton's mobility failed to overcome an offense that struggled to protect him or generate consistent rushing production.

Milton completed 18 of 34 passes for 169 yards without a touchdown or interception, finishing with a 66.9 passer rating. He also led Philadelphia with 64 yards on nine rushing attempts and scored a two-point conversion. The production included useful flashes, but seven sacks and a lost fumble limited his effectiveness.

Milton's best early sequence came during Philadelphia's eight-play, 58-yard touchdown drive. A 19-yard scramble on third down kept the possession alive, and a throw toward Darius Cooper drew a pass-interference penalty that moved the Eagles into scoring position.

Saquon Barkley finished with a 3-yard touchdown run. After a Giants penalty on the extra-point attempt, Philadelphia went for two, and Milton converted before celebrating with an end zone backflip.

The Eagles led 8-6, but that possession produced their only touchdown.

Makai Lemon caught six passes for 61 yards, while Dallas Goedert added five receptions for 50 yards. Cooper finished with two catches for 25 yards despite eight targets.

Milton's longest completion covered 20 yards. Philadelphia needed more productive early-down passing and more completions that created manageable third downs. Instead, the Eagles converted five of 18 third-down attempts and repeatedly returned the ball to New York.

Milton lost 41 yards on seven sacks, and Arvell Reese's strip-sack erased an opportunity created by Philadelphia's recovery of a muffed punt. The Eagles finished with only 128 net passing yards.

The protection problems make the evaluation more complicated than the passing line alone. Milton must recognize pressure and get the ball out when opportunities exist, but Philadelphia also must provide a functioning structure around him.

Milton's running ability is a useful addition, especially for an offense searching for ways to extend possessions. It cannot carry the entire operation. Barkley and Elijah Mitchell combined for 28 rushing yards, leaving Milton responsible for most of the ground production.

The Eagles now have a bye to review his decisions, protection responses, and passing opportunities. His first start provided reasons to keep developing him, but it offered little evidence that changing quarterbacks alone will repair Philadelphia's offense.

#2674. Pick your poison: Rams' Myles Garrett anticipates matchup nightmares in first game with Aaron Donald

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When Los Angeles Rams edge rusher Myles Garrett returns from injured reserve this week for his first game action since the season opener, he will line up next to defensive lineman Aaron Donald for the first time. That duo is projected to be one of the NFL's most unstoppable tandems at any position since Donald announced that he would come out of retirement for the 2026 season, and now the league will find out just how formidable it really is.

The timing of Garrett's IR stint and Donald's season debut clashed, forcing them to wait until November to suit up together. Garrett played just one game before he underwent knee surgery, and Donald entered the lineup in Week 2.

Garrett said it will be surreal to share the field with a fellow Defensive Player of the Year award winner.

"Going into this season, I never thought I'd have the chance," Garrett said ahead of Sunday's road game against the Washington Commanders. "As y'all know, he kept us in suspense for quite a while. It was very exciting to hear about that. Looking forward to the opportunity to get on the field and actually play some real snaps with him."

Garrett's arrival in Los Angeles by way of a blockbuster trade in June was a catalyst for Donald's unretirement, so it is only right that two of the most disruptive players in football history finally get the opportunity to play alongside each other. Donald has been more effective in run defense than pass rushing this season, so with Garrett (the single-season sack record holder) rejoining the fold, their skill sets should complement each other tremendously.

Both superstar defenders have commanded double teams at extreme rates throughout their careers, but opposing offensive lines might have to stay more honest with their assignments so as to prevent the other player from capitalizing on the diverted attention.

"I think offenses really have to pick their poison," Garrett said. "Who's going to be freed up this play? Either of us are pretty good at winning one-on-ones. We'll have some fun."

There is no better time than the present for Garrett to return to full strength and for this duo to join forces. The Rams are in the midst of a potential midseason turnaround after opening the year with a surprising yet immensely disappointing 2-4 record, and they need to keep the momentum rolling to fulfill their Super Bowl expectations.

At the time, it was a surprise to see Garrett held entirely in check in the season-opening blowout loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. When the news of his knee ailment came to light, though, it explained why he was held without a single tackle in the contest. Garrett said that the knee acted up on him throughout the game and limited him from making his typical impact as a first-team All-Pro-caliber force off the edge.

Now that he is healthy, the question is just how great of an impact Garrett will make for the elite Rams defense. Every year since his rookie season, the former No. 1 overall pick has logged double-digit sacks. Last season, he broke the NFL single-season record with 23. He is also a stalwart in run defense and led the league in tackles of loss each of the last two years.

There was one sign in Week 1 that suggested Garrett will deliver his usual impact and perhaps even take another step forward in his first year with the Rams. He logged five quarterback pressures on Brock Purdy in that loss to the 49ers, good for an 18.5% pressure rate on his 39 defensive snaps. That would be the third-best mark of his career if it sustained over a full season.

#2673. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2671. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

#2670. Tennessee football fans eager to see the Faizon Brandon package, CFP climb past Alabama

Tennessee football fans want to see more Faizon Brandon in the offense, DeSean Bishop's assault on the record book and the Vols climb the College Football Playoff rankings.

They should get all three wishes granted as the No. 9 Vols head into the final three-game stretch of the regular season. They also want an explanation for a controversial call that they thought was a UT touchdown by DaSaahn Brame.

Tennessee (7-2, 4-2 SEC) plays at Texas A&M (4-5, 1-5) on Nov. 14 (3 p.m. ET, ESPN). But first, let's look back to UT's 34-6 win over No. 13 Kentucky by answering fan questions in an overflowing Vols mailbag.

Supposedly, the CFP rankings reset each week. But judging by the initial CFP Top 25, Tennessee should move up four spots because four teams ahead of the Vols lost. No. 8 BYU lost to No. 3 Utah. No. 10 Ole Miss lost to No. 2 Georgia. No. 12 Ohio State lost to No. 23 Oregon. Plus, No. 13 Tennessee beat No. 6 Kentucky – that is, according to the CFP rankings.

Georgia, Utah and Alabama might be the top three. There'll be an ongoing debate about the weight of UT's head-to-head 26-10 win over Alabama. But the important thing for the Vols is that they keep winning to secure a playoff spot.

In Tennessee's case, yes. The Vols have quality wins over playoff contenders Alabama and Kentucky and "good" losses to Texas and South Carolina. That's a strong résumé.

If UT wins its remaining games to finish 10-2, it'll likely host one of the first-round games, which go to seeds 5-8.

If UT loses a close game at Texas A&M and then beats LSU and Vanderbilt to finish 9-3, there still could be a narrow path to the playoff, depending on how the rest of the SEC finishes.

Good question. It's confusing because only the CFP committee knows exactly where that so-called "pod" of top-tier teams ends.

I think Alabama, Texas and Tennessee should be clustered together. That's how voters in the US LBM Coaches Poll and AP Top 25 saw it. They placed Alabama at No. 7, Texas as No. 8 and Tennessee at No. 9.

Head-to-head results aren't the only factor in ranking teams, but it should be a major one. That being said, Alabama has a strong résumé, including the No. 1 strength of schedule and good road wins.

You're referring to the ESPN Playoff Predictor featured on SEC Network. That takes into account each team's probability of winning its remaining games. In other words, that prediction model believes that UT will lose at least one more game. If UT wins out for a 10-2 record, the probability increases to nearly 100%.

For now, UT should get credit for beating a good team because Kentucky remains in playoff contention. With only two losses, UK likely would make the playoff if it can beat Florida, Missouri and Louisville to finish 10-2.

Bishop has 196 rushing attempts for 1,066 yards and 13 touchdowns with three regular-season games and at least one postseason game remaining.

Travis Stephens owns UT's single-season record with 291 carries in 2001. Bishop hasn't cracked the top 10 yet, but he ultimately could challenge Stephens' mark.

Dylan Sampson rushed for 1,491 yards in 2024 for that record. Bishop ranks 18th, but he's on pace to finish with more than 1,500 yards if he can remain healthy and productive.

Sampson scored 22 rushing TDs in 2024. Bishop is tied for eighth, but he needs only five TDs to move into second place and then challenge Sampson's mark.

It seemed that way, but that's because no UT offensive player played much in the first half. The Vols had only 22 offensive snaps in the first half, and Bishop carried the ball on nine of those.

Coach Josh Heupel likes stats, and Bishop got his fifth straight 100-yard game by carrying the ball on those last two plays. But I can't say that Heupel considered that.

Bishop was well rested, and he is UT's preferred closer for wins like that. He finished with 25 carries, which is a moderate workload compared to his recent output.

It was rolled out very effectively. There was a handoff on Brandon's first play, but that introduced the package to Kentucky's defense. His 29-yard run flashed what Brandon can do on a quarterback sweep. And that set up the 24-yard TD on a shovel pass to Mike Matthews, which worked off the same action as the earlier quarterback sweep.

There's a progression to that package, and UT did it wonderfully. Now the next phase is adding a passing option to it, which I'm sure the Vols already have.

Yes, I think so. George MacIntyre still gives UT the best chance to win as the starting quarterback. He made a few good passes, including a couple that were dropped. And he's improving in all areas of the passing game, although some of that improvement isn't easily perceptible.

But UT needs productive wrinkles in its offense, and Brandon has that potential. Against Kentucky, he was a running threat with creative play calls. But he is also an accurate passer, albeit perhaps limited in working through progressions against complex coverages.

Brandon's growing pains are understandable for a freshman, but his talent is also undeniable. UT should utilize it in select situations.

I understand that sentiment. But I think there's a tendency for fans to nitpick victories of their own team but overlook blemishes of other teams. It's understandable because fans live and die on every play of their team.

However, fans of other teams periodically checked into Tennessee's game and took away that it was a rout because that's what the score said.

Also, the manner in which the Vols win shouldn't be devalued. Their 21-0 fourth-quarter surge wasn't accidental. It was earned with a physical style of play through the first three quarters.

Heupel said he challenged the running backs at halftime because they had missed some assignments and running lanes set up by blocks. They refocused and reconfigured, and it showed in the results. The Vols rushed for 134 yards in the second half.

In the third quarter, Brame caught a 20-yard pass and fell backward over the goal line as he tried to secure the ball. He didn't lose possession until he landed in the end zone. However, ESPN rules analyst Steve Shaw, the former SEC head of officials, explained during the broadcast why it was an incomplete pass.

When a receiver is going to the ground as they make a catch – diving or falling, for example – they must maintain possession through contact with the ground. So it looked like a catch but wasn't one, by rule.

Bad calls have always existed in college football. Video replay and multiple TV angles have exposed them more often these days. But I don't think UT has been a victim of bad calls any more than other teams. For example, some of the loudest boos at Neyland Stadium came after Matthews was flagged for offensive pass interference, but it was the correct call.

Yes. The game plan dictates how that expansion is displayed. But against Kentucky, a few vertical routes opened up against man coverage as UT utilized play-action fakes. MacIntyre completed a 34-yarder to Braylon Staley and a 36-yarder to Radarious Jackson. He overthrew Staley on another deep pass. The throw to Brame was exceptional, but it didn't yield a touchdown.

Defensive end Tyree Weathersby and Brame left the game with injuries. Heupel did not have an update on their condition after the game. Weathersby's injury looked serious, but that's not an official medical diagnosis.

Weathersby leads the team with seven sacks and two fumble recoveries, so he's a valuable weapon on defense. The SEC availability report for the Texas A&M game will be released on Nov. 11.

It's hard to say, but I wonder if that was a miscommunication or pre-snap misread by MacIntyre. UT had four receivers split wide, presumably to spread out UK's defense and lighten the tackle box. That would've given Bishop room to run.

Instead, UK put seven defenders in the tackle box and had only four defensive backs to defend four receivers. If there was an option to pass out of that formation, that seemed like a better option in that situation. But MacIntyre handed the ball to Bishop for no gain.

The answer is different depending on the play. UK sometimes caught UT in man coverage with no spy mirroring the quarterback. Sometimes the spy didn't immediately make the tackle. Also, give UK quarterback Kenny Minchey credit for evading the pass rush in a few instances.

But while it seemed like Minchey had a string of successful scrambles, there actually weren't that many. He had six rushing attempts for 33 yards. He broke a 12-yard scramble and a pair of 7-yard scrambles. Otherwise, he was dropped for four sacks and a couple of minimal gains.

That might depend on LSU's mindset when it comes to Knoxville on Nov. 21. LSU drifted out of the playoff pool after a 31-13 home loss to Alabama and no Top 25 wins.

LSU could perhaps get back in it with back-to-back wins over Texas and Tennessee. But if the Tigers lose to Texas, they could be unmotivated for the Tennessee game.

Texas A&M will be a challenge because it's an SEC road game. But again, the question is how focused the Aggies are. The perspective of the opponent matters as much as UT's approach.

I predicted an 8-4 record in the preseason.

I think 9-3 or 10-2 seem more likely now. That includes a win over Vanderbilt and either a sweep or split of the Texas A&M and LSU games. If the Vols don't make the playoff, a consolation prize might be a Florida bowl.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

#2667. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2666. NFL fines Jaquan Brisker, two others for illegal Week 8 hits that placed opponents in concussion protocol

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL levied 31 fines in Week 8, which was the second most in a single week this season. Among the most notable punishments were those handed down to Pittsburgh Steelers safety Jaquan Brisker, Dallas Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown and Las Vegas Raiders safety Jeremy Chinn. Each fine was the result of a hit that led to the offensive player being placed in concussion protocol and ruled out for Week 9.

Brisker owes the NFL $17,911 for a blow to the head/neck on Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson. The play occurred less than a minute and a half into the Steelers' victory and drew a roughing the passer penalty, which Brisker voiced extreme displeasure with after the game.

"Babying the quarterback," Brisker said. "He's laying there crying, whatever he was doing. It is what it is. I assume I'm going to get fined because if you watch it, I'm hitting him with my chest and them I'm off to the side. But he had his binky today, so they threw it out there. It is what it is."

Watson briefly left the game, and Shedeur Sanders replaced him. The latter threw two passes before Watson returned to action and finished the game. Although Watson practiced in the days leading up to this Sunday's matchup against the New Orleans Saints and cleared the concussion protocol on Saturday, the Browns announced they will turn to Sanders as their Week 9 starter.

Brisker flagged for hit on Watson #Steelers #NFL pic.twitter.com/FCOv8QtjJA

Overshown's fine is for his use of his helmet on a hit against Arizona Cardinals running back Bam Knight. He must pay $9,528. The hit jarred the ball loose from Knight's hands, and the Cowboys recovered the fumble without a penalty. The NFL reviewed the play in the wake of the game, however, and issued the fine.

Knight will not play in the Cardinals' divisional clash with the Seattle Seahawks. He did not practice this week.

Two different angles of the hit on #AZCardinals RB Bam Knight pic.twitter.com/i2zS8LzGyF

Chinn sealed a Raiders win last week with an interception in the end zone, but just one play prior, he made forcible contact with New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson on a catch along the sideline, which resulted in a fine. Chinn owes $17,911 for a hit on a defenseless player. The two players' helmets collided on the play, and while Wilson stayed in the game for the Jets' final snap, he later entered concussion protocol.

Wilson reported concussion symptoms the next day, and by midweek the Jets placed him in the protocol. They eventually ruled him out for this week's battle with the Kansas City Chiefs.

Garrett Wilson Somehow, Someway Hangs On To This Ball.Then Jeremy Chinn Goes Helmet To Helmet And Blows Him Up.What A Dirty Play. 😡 pic.twitter.com/Og7SwQWrqZ

There have been 223 plays this season which resulted in a fine. That is 0.0113% of all plays through eight weeks. The 31 fines from Week 8 were second only to the 38 in Week 2.

The winners of the 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove were announced Sunday night by Major League Baseball and, as expected, Cubs wunderkind Pete Crow-Armstrong took home his second straight National League Gold Glove in center field. PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. This means, obviously, that postseason performance had no impact. Here now are the 2026 Gold Glove winners.

#2663. Tennessee football fans eager to see the Faizon Brandon package, CFP climb past Alabama

Tennessee football fans want to see more Faizon Brandon in the offense, DeSean Bishop's assault on the record book and the Vols climb the College Football Playoff rankings.

They should get all three wishes granted as the No. 9 Vols head into the final three-game stretch of the regular season. They also want an explanation for a controversial call that they thought was a UT touchdown by DaSaahn Brame.

Tennessee (7-2, 4-2 SEC) plays at Texas A&M (4-5, 1-5) on Nov. 14 (3 p.m. ET, ESPN). But first, let's look back to UT's 34-6 win over No. 13 Kentucky by answering fan questions in an overflowing Vols mailbag.

Supposedly, the CFP rankings reset each week. But judging by the initial CFP Top 25, Tennessee should move up four spots because four teams ahead of the Vols lost. No. 8 BYU lost to No. 3 Utah. No. 10 Ole Miss lost to No. 2 Georgia. No. 12 Ohio State lost to No. 23 Oregon. Plus, No. 13 Tennessee beat No. 6 Kentucky – that is, according to the CFP rankings.

Georgia, Utah and Alabama might be the top three. There'll be an ongoing debate about the weight of UT's head-to-head 26-10 win over Alabama. But the important thing for the Vols is that they keep winning to secure a playoff spot.

In Tennessee's case, yes. The Vols have quality wins over playoff contenders Alabama and Kentucky and "good" losses to Texas and South Carolina. That's a strong résumé.

If UT wins its remaining games to finish 10-2, it'll likely host one of the first-round games, which go to seeds 5-8.

If UT loses a close game at Texas A&M and then beats LSU and Vanderbilt to finish 9-3, there still could be a narrow path to the playoff, depending on how the rest of the SEC finishes.

Good question. It's confusing because only the CFP committee knows exactly where that so-called "pod" of top-tier teams ends.

I think Alabama, Texas and Tennessee should be clustered together. That's how voters in the US LBM Coaches Poll and AP Top 25 saw it. They placed Alabama at No. 7, Texas as No. 8 and Tennessee at No. 9.

Head-to-head results aren't the only factor in ranking teams, but it should be a major one. That being said, Alabama has a strong résumé, including the No. 1 strength of schedule and good road wins.

You're referring to the ESPN Playoff Predictor featured on SEC Network. That takes into account each team's probability of winning its remaining games. In other words, that prediction model believes that UT will lose at least one more game. If UT wins out for a 10-2 record, the probability increases to nearly 100%.

For now, UT should get credit for beating a good team because Kentucky remains in playoff contention. With only two losses, UK likely would make the playoff if it can beat Florida, Missouri and Louisville to finish 10-2.

Bishop has 196 rushing attempts for 1,066 yards and 13 touchdowns with three regular-season games and at least one postseason game remaining.

Travis Stephens owns UT's single-season record with 291 carries in 2001. Bishop hasn't cracked the top 10 yet, but he ultimately could challenge Stephens' mark.

Dylan Sampson rushed for 1,491 yards in 2024 for that record. Bishop ranks 18th, but he's on pace to finish with more than 1,500 yards if he can remain healthy and productive.

Sampson scored 22 rushing TDs in 2024. Bishop is tied for eighth, but he needs only five TDs to move into second place and then challenge Sampson's mark.

It seemed that way, but that's because no UT offensive player played much in the first half. The Vols had only 22 offensive snaps in the first half, and Bishop carried the ball on nine of those.

Coach Josh Heupel likes stats, and Bishop got his fifth straight 100-yard game by carrying the ball on those last two plays. But I can't say that Heupel considered that.

Bishop was well rested, and he is UT's preferred closer for wins like that. He finished with 25 carries, which is a moderate workload compared to his recent output.

It was rolled out very effectively. There was a handoff on Brandon's first play, but that introduced the package to Kentucky's defense. His 29-yard run flashed what Brandon can do on a quarterback sweep. And that set up the 24-yard TD on a shovel pass to Mike Matthews, which worked off the same action as the earlier quarterback sweep.

There's a progression to that package, and UT did it wonderfully. Now the next phase is adding a passing option to it, which I'm sure the Vols already have.

Yes, I think so. George MacIntyre still gives UT the best chance to win as the starting quarterback. He made a few good passes, including a couple that were dropped. And he's improving in all areas of the passing game, although some of that improvement isn't easily perceptible.

But UT needs productive wrinkles in its offense, and Brandon has that potential. Against Kentucky, he was a running threat with creative play calls. But he is also an accurate passer, albeit perhaps limited in working through progressions against complex coverages.

Brandon's growing pains are understandable for a freshman, but his talent is also undeniable. UT should utilize it in select situations.

I understand that sentiment. But I think there's a tendency for fans to nitpick victories of their own team but overlook blemishes of other teams. It's understandable because fans live and die on every play of their team.

However, fans of other teams periodically checked into Tennessee's game and took away that it was a rout because that's what the score said.

Also, the manner in which the Vols win shouldn't be devalued. Their 21-0 fourth-quarter surge wasn't accidental. It was earned with a physical style of play through the first three quarters.

Heupel said he challenged the running backs at halftime because they had missed some assignments and running lanes set up by blocks. They refocused and reconfigured, and it showed in the results. The Vols rushed for 134 yards in the second half.

In the third quarter, Brame caught a 20-yard pass and fell backward over the goal line as he tried to secure the ball. He didn't lose possession until he landed in the end zone. However, ESPN rules analyst Steve Shaw, the former SEC head of officials, explained during the broadcast why it was an incomplete pass.

When a receiver is going to the ground as they make a catch – diving or falling, for example – they must maintain possession through contact with the ground. So it looked like a catch but wasn't one, by rule.

Bad calls have always existed in college football. Video replay and multiple TV angles have exposed them more often these days. But I don't think UT has been a victim of bad calls any more than other teams. For example, some of the loudest boos at Neyland Stadium came after Matthews was flagged for offensive pass interference, but it was the correct call.

Yes. The game plan dictates how that expansion is displayed. But against Kentucky, a few vertical routes opened up against man coverage as UT utilized play-action fakes. MacIntyre completed a 34-yarder to Braylon Staley and a 36-yarder to Radarious Jackson. He overthrew Staley on another deep pass. The throw to Brame was exceptional, but it didn't yield a touchdown.

Defensive end Tyree Weathersby and Brame left the game with injuries. Heupel did not have an update on their condition after the game. Weathersby's injury looked serious, but that's not an official medical diagnosis.

Weathersby leads the team with seven sacks and two fumble recoveries, so he's a valuable weapon on defense. The SEC availability report for the Texas A&M game will be released on Nov. 11.

It's hard to say, but I wonder if that was a miscommunication or pre-snap misread by MacIntyre. UT had four receivers split wide, presumably to spread out UK's defense and lighten the tackle box. That would've given Bishop room to run.

Instead, UK put seven defenders in the tackle box and had only four defensive backs to defend four receivers. If there was an option to pass out of that formation, that seemed like a better option in that situation. But MacIntyre handed the ball to Bishop for no gain.

The answer is different depending on the play. UK sometimes caught UT in man coverage with no spy mirroring the quarterback. Sometimes the spy didn't immediately make the tackle. Also, give UK quarterback Kenny Minchey credit for evading the pass rush in a few instances.

But while it seemed like Minchey had a string of successful scrambles, there actually weren't that many. He had six rushing attempts for 33 yards. He broke a 12-yard scramble and a pair of 7-yard scrambles. Otherwise, he was dropped for four sacks and a couple of minimal gains.

That might depend on LSU's mindset when it comes to Knoxville on Nov. 21. LSU drifted out of the playoff pool after a 31-13 home loss to Alabama and no Top 25 wins.

LSU could perhaps get back in it with back-to-back wins over Texas and Tennessee. But if the Tigers lose to Texas, they could be unmotivated for the Tennessee game.

Texas A&M will be a challenge because it's an SEC road game. But again, the question is how focused the Aggies are. The perspective of the opponent matters as much as UT's approach.

I predicted an 8-4 record in the preseason.

I think 9-3 or 10-2 seem more likely now. That includes a win over Vanderbilt and either a sweep or split of the Texas A&M and LSU games. If the Vols don't make the playoff, a consolation prize might be a Florida bowl.

Two of the NFL's hottest teams will clash Sunday night in the Windy City when the Chicago Bears host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Here's how you can follow the action, along with a breakdown and a prediction.

Chicago's offense has been a juggernaut since Caleb Williams returned from injury. Over that span, they've scored 31, 30 and 34 points while receiving stellar play from Williams, who has re-entered the league MVP conversation.

Over the last three games, Williams has completed a staggering 73.8% of his passes with four touchdowns and zero picks while averaging 287 yards per game.

Last Sunday was Jeffery Simmons' first game as a Bear after he was traded from Tennessee. Against the Seahawks, Simmons filled the stat sheet with six tackles (including one for loss), a sack and a pass breakup. Simmons was part of a Bears defense that held Seattle to just 17 points, 18 first downs and 252 yards.

Jeffery Simmons highlights, anyone? pic.twitter.com/AwU17TzjfC

Williams will have to rise to the challenge of facing a Buccaneer defense that is conjuring up memories of Tampa Bay's legendary "Tampa 2" unit.

Over the last two games, the Buccaneers' defense has allowed just 13 points and forced a whopping eight turnovers. They've been especially stout against the pass, allowing just 175 and 125 yards in their last two games. Tampa Bay has also held their last two opponents (the Panthers and Falcons) to under 100 rushing yards, which is significant given the running backs (Chuba Hubbard and Bijan Robinson) they've faced in recent weeks.

The Buccaneers' defensive charge has been led by linebackers Josiah Trotter (68 tackles and a pick-six), Alex Anzalone (42 tackles and three interceptions) and pass rushers David Walker and YaYa Diaby.

Along with their defense, the Buccaneers' recent success has been predicated on the running game and specifically running backs Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell. Tampa Bay ran for 258 yards in its 43-13 win over Carolina and 324 in the rain during last Sunday's 16-0 win over Atlanta while becoming the first team since 1974 to win a game without completing a pass.

Irving ran for a career-high 170 yards against Atlanta while recording his third 100-yard rushing performance in Tampa Bay's last four games. Gainwell ran for a career-high 140 yards and 25 carries against the Falcons.

After a 0-4 start, Tampa Bay has proven to be a team on the rise over the past month. The Buccaneers are first in the NFL in both rushing yards gained and fewest rushing yards allowed.

Tampa Bay's passing game, however, has largely been non-existent, even with the return of Baker Mayfield. Until Tampa Bay's passing game starts to show its teeth, it's going to be hard to pick them in matchups like this.

I'm picking the Bears in a game that will likely come down to defense and Caleb Williams making a few key completions down the stretch. Score: Bears 20, Buccaneers 16

#2660. MLB Power Rankings: Brewers end 2026 season at No. 1 as World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

It's a juggernaut of an organization. They churn out talent and get the most out of every player they have. They seem to trade away talent at the exact right time. They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

The Brewers head to next season with plenty of question marks, but they'll answer them. They always do. They are the champions of Major League Baseball and they sit atop the final 2026 Power Rankings.

Looking forward to next spring, my expectation is the Brewers will be No. 1. Some years, I write about why the defending champion is not No. 1. I've long since learned my lesson with this team, though. No more. The Brewers will be No. 1 heading into spring training.

Following a week without an international game, the NFL heads back overseas in Week 9 when it sends the Atlanta Falcons and Cincinnati Bengals to Spain. The Bernabéu will play host to American football for the second time in as many years as two divisional contenders descend upon Madrid.

The Bengals are in search of their first win away from American soil in franchise history after going 0-1-1 in their previous two opportunities (the most recent contest dating back to 2019), while the Falcons seek to improve to .500 in games abroad. Atlanta is 2-3 away from the United States and last season lost in Berlin.

This contest pits one of the league's hottest teams against a squad that aims to reestablish positive momentum. Cincinnati rides a three-game win streak into the Madrid Game and scored no fewer than 31 points in any of those triumphs, albeit with two of the matchups coming against bottom-tier competition. Atlanta, on the other hand, lost in two of its last three outings and went scoreless in its most recent showing.

Both sides are alive and well in their respective divisions, but the context between the two differs greatly. The Falcons are just a half game back of first place in the NFC South, which may be the weakest division in football with no teams at or above .500 through the season's first two months. The Bengals' position at half a game out of the AFC North lead is the superior standing considering three teams own winning records.

Fans of American football in Spain are in for a treat, because this game has all the makings of a shootout. There is not an offense in the NFL that is clicking quite like the Bengals over the last three weeks, and between Burrow, Chase, Higgins, London and Robinson, five of the biggest names in football will be in action in a star-studded battle. Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr. should bounce back from last week's dreadful 8-for-24 showing in the rain, so Atlanta ought to have enough juice to keep pace with a team that is averaging 36.3 points per game since Oct. 11.

In a matchup where points will be aplenty, the team with the better defense holds the edge. It is not as though Atlanta is vastly superior on that side of the ball, but it is much more reliable and is about to insert one of its projected top producers into the lineup for the first time this season. There is not a more opportune time for a disruptive pass rusher like Pearce to make his first appearance than against arguably the best quarterback in the NFL. #2653. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.

#2651. NBA Rumor: Why Trading Naz Reid For Scoot Henderson Makes Zero Sense For Charlotte

Social media speculation moves fast across the league, and a recent NBA rumor floating a trade between the Portland Trail Blazers and the Charlotte Hornets has generated plenty of online chatter. The proposed framework features Portland sending fourth-year guard Scoot Henderson, draft capital centered on the Orlando Magic's 2028 first-round pick, and salary filler to Charlotte in exchange for Naz Reid.

On the surface, it is easy to see why observers might connect those dots. Charlotte's perimeter depth is severely tested, secondary guard options are sidelined, and the backcourt is taking nightly beatings. However, while acquiring a high-lottery guard and a future draft pick sounds enticing on a broadcast, evaluating Charlotte's actual timeline and roster makeup reveals why this trade makes zero sense.

The main issue with bringing in Henderson isn't about belittling his talent—it comes down to fit on a Hornets roster that is missing LaMelo Ball's offense.

Henderson possesses raw downhill athleticism, but he remains a high-variance guard who needs high usage to operate while still trying to establish consistent perimeter shooting.

Through his early NBA career, Henderson has struggled with three-point efficiency and decision-making in high-leverage possessions. Charlotte's offense is already drowning in heavy turnover numbers. Adding another non-spacing ball-handler who turns the ball over at a high rate doesn't fix Charlotte's half-court execution; it simply compounds the mess.

Furthermore, Henderson's point-of-attack defense hasn't reached a level where he can hold up without heavy backline support. Swapping a functional piece for a developing guard who adds more spacing friction to the floor doesn't help what Charles Lee is trying to establish.

Trading Reid creates an immediate, unnecessary hole in Charlotte's frontcourt. Reid isn't saving this franchise, but he is a productive, modern big who can shoot from deep, handle in secondary actions, and play multiple frontcourt spots. If Charlotte ships Reid to Portland, the squad is left without a single starter-level power forward capable of stretching defenses and making plays off the bounce.

Also, Reid gives Charlotte the ability to run versatile big-man pairings or slide into standalone center looks. Stripping the frontcourt of one of its floor-spacing options just to hoard more guard depth destroys what little functional structure this offense has.

Nov 6, 2026; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Charlotte Hornets center Naz Reid (0) takes the rebound up court against the Boston Celtics during the first half at Spectrum Center. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images

Proponents of the rumor highlight Portland, including the Magic's 2028 first-round pick, as the key draft sweetener to get a deal done. Future draft picks are always useful, but a distant 2028 first-round pick does nothing for Charlotte's immediate day-to-day development.

Jeff Peterson made the franchise's direction clear when he traded away Ball in the offseason and preached patience for a long-term build. Charlotte knows this season is going to be rough. But taking on a reclamation project in Henderson while stripping the roster of frontcourt spacing for a distant draft pick isn't rebuilding—it's just accumulating random parts without a blueprint.

It is easy to get reactive when injuries pile up, and the losses get ugly. Between Brandon Miller exiting with a groin injury, Kon Knueppel's hamstring strain, and secondary guard absences, the backcourt looks paper-thin. However, panicking into a trade for a guard who doesn't fit the floor isn't the answer.

This season was always going to be about taking hits and establishing habits. Charlotte isn't fighting for a playoff spot, and trading away solid frontcourt pieces for a high-turnover guard and distant picks won't speed up the timeline.

While Portland would gladly take Reid's frontcourt versatility off Charlotte's hands, the Hornets have no reason to bite. Henderson's game doesn't fix Charlotte's half-court flaws, a 2028 pick doesn't replace starter-level frontcourt minutes, and losing Reid leaves the roster completely empty at power forward.

Charlotte needs to take its lumps, stay patient, and ignore trade frameworks that make a bad situation worse.
